pages.title: Text back every missed call automatically for an HVAC business

steps: Connect your business phone system (a VoIP service such as OpenPhone, Dialpad or a Twilio number) so it fires a webhook or Zapier trigger on missed calls.

Log every reply to your CRM or a Google Sheet.
Forward the reply to the on-call technician's phone.

pages.title: Cut clinic no-shows with a layered appointment reminder sequence
pages.summary: Send a booking confirmation, then reminders about 48–72 hours out, 24 hours out (with confirm/reschedule), and a short same-day logistics text. Keep SMS to date, time and clinic name—no diagnoses—and use a vendor that will sign a BAA.
steps: Confirm how your practice management or EHR already sends reminders. Turn on built-in reminders first if they cover confirmation and day-before texts; only add Zapier/Make/n8n for gaps.
Collect mobile numbers and written consent for appointment texts at registration. Document channel preferences and honor STOP and reasonable confidential-communication requests.

Build a layered cadence keyed to the live schedule: immediate booking confirmation (date, time, location or telehealth link, how to reschedule); a 48–72 hour reminder; a 24-hour two-way confirm/reschedule text; a short same-day logistics text 2–4 hours before.
Keep every unencrypted SMS minimal: patient first name optional, clinic name, date/time, confirm or reschedule instructions. No diagnoses, results, procedure details or clinical notes.
Stop the sequence when the visit is cancelled, rescheduled or completed. Sync status from the schedule before every send so you never remind for a dead slot.
After a no-show, send one polite rebook link and create a staff task—no blame language. Review no-show and confirmation rates monthly.

p: Tools: your practice management/EHR or booking calendar + a HIPAA-ready messaging vendor (with a signed BAA) and/or Zapier/Make/n8n + SMS/email. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page.

On answering machines or shared phones, leave only what is needed to confirm the appointment (for example clinic name and callback number), not clinical detail.
If a patient asks for an alternate contact method or location, honor reasonable requests.
Text only numbers you have consent for, identify the clinic, and honor STOP. Prefer a vendor with a Business Associate Agreement rather than a consumer SMS app.

pages.summary: When a shopper who already opted into SMS leaves items in cart, send one reminder within 48 hours with a link back to checkout. Use double opt-in, disclose cart reminders in your signup terms, and never collect payment by text.

Update your mobile terms and privacy policy to say you track abandoned carts (for example via cookies or your cart plugin) and may send SMS cart reminders to opted-in subscribers.
In Shopify, WooCommerce or your cart tool, trigger when a cart or checkout is abandoned and the shopper is an active SMS subscriber (opted in before abandonment).
Send exactly one SMS per abandonment event, within 48 hours. Include your business name, a short cart nudge, a direct link to the cart/checkout page, and STOP instructions.
Do not complete the purchase by text, collect card data by SMS, or accept a keyword as payment approval—the customer must pay on your site.
Log consent, send time and STOP replies. Keep sends inside quiet hours for the shopper's time zone, and stop if they opt out.

US carriers commonly require double opt-in, one SMS per abandoned-cart event, and send within 48 hours for this use case.

pages.summary: Before you send holiday promotions, make sure your domain is authenticated (SPF or DKIM at minimum, ideally SPF, DKIM and DMARC) and that marketing emails have an easy unsubscribe. Gmail requires this for senders, and unauthenticated mail may go to spam or be rejected, so it's a 30-minute check that protects your best sales weeks.

p: Your holiday offers reach the inbox instead of spam, and it gets harder for scammers to send email that pretends to be you.

ul: Google's sender guidelines say everyone sending to personal Gmail accounts must set up SPF or DKIM, and Google recommends always setting up SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

If you send more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail accounts, SPF, DKIM and DMARC are all required, and marketing messages must support one-click unsubscribe and show a clear unsubscribe link in the body.
Google says messages that aren't authenticated this way might be marked as spam or rejected.
Google asks senders to keep the spam rate shown in Postmaster Tools below 0.10% and never let it reach 0.30%.

ol: List every tool that sends email as your domain: your mailbox (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365), your newsletter tool, and any booking, invoicing or website-form app.
In each tool, find its domain authentication setting and add the DNS records it gives you at your domain host. Your SPF record should include every service that sends for you.
Add a DMARC record. Google says the policy can start at "none". Turn on DMARC reports so you can see who sends mail using your domain.
Send a test email to a Gmail address, open it, and choose More, then Show original. Check that SPF, DKIM and DMARC say PASS.
Open one of your marketing emails and confirm there's a visible unsubscribe link. Ask your email tool whether it adds one-click unsubscribe headers (most marketing tools handle this for you).
Sign up for Google Postmaster Tools to watch your spam rate through the season.

ul: Back up your current DNS records before you change anything. A wrong SPF or DKIM edit can stop your everyday email from arriving.
Only email people who signed up. Google's guidelines say not to buy email lists or send to people who didn't sign up.
This covers deliverability, not the law. US commercial email also has to follow the FTC's CAN-SPAM rules.

pages.summary: Type your offer, end date and code as real text near the top of promo emails instead of baking them into one graphic. Outlook blocks downloaded pictures by default, Apple Mail and Gmail can show AI summaries, and screen readers can't read words inside an image.

p: More people see your deal: shoppers whose email app hides images, people skimming an AI-written preview on their phone, and customers who use a screen reader.

ul: Classic Outlook is set by default to block automatic picture downloads from the internet, and Outlook for Mac doesn't download internet pictures by default either. If your offer lives inside an image, those readers see a blank box until they click.
On iPhones with Apple Intelligence turned on, Apple Mail shows a short summary under each email in the inbox instead of the first lines of the message.
Gmail can show an AI Overview at the top of an email that sums up its key points.
Email agency Backstroke says these AI summaries work from an email's live text, so an offer that appears only inside an image can be left out of the summary.
The W3C's accessibility guidelines say to use real text instead of pictures of text, and that when an image does contain text, its alt text should repeat the same words.

ol: Open your last promo email in your email tool's preview with images turned off. Can you still tell what the offer is, when it ends and how to redeem it?
Rewrite the top of the email in real text: the offer, the end date, the code, and whether it works in store, online or both.
Keep your graphic as decoration. If it has words in it, give it alt text with the same words.
Make your main button a real text button in your email editor, not a picture of a button.
Put the offer in the subject line and preview text too.
Send a test to yourself on an iPhone and in Gmail, and check that the preview or summary mentions the offer.

ul: AI summaries can get things wrong, and you can't control what they say. Clear, short text at the top is your best bet.
Put exclusions and fine print in real text as well, so nobody misses them.
Whether people see these summaries depends on their device, settings, language and account, so don't promise customers what their inbox will show.

pages.summary: Pull this year's payments to non-employees from your bookkeeping tool, flag anyone you'll likely need to send a 1099-NEC to, and send each one a secure W-9 request with automatic reminders until it's on file. steps: Export this year's payments to contractors and other non-employees from QuickBooks, Xero or your bank: payee name, email, total paid so far, and whether you already have a W-9 on file.

For each flagged payee with no W-9 on file, have Zapier, Make or n8n send a short email asking them to upload the current IRS Form W-9 through a secure upload link (your accounting software's vendor portal, a secure form tool, or your accountant's client portal). Never ask for the form or a Social Security number by plain email reply.

When a W-9 arrives, the upload tool's "new file" trigger marks the row "received" and stops the reminders. Someone on your team checks that the name and taxpayer ID box are filled in and the form is signed.
Send up to two reminders a week apart, then put anyone still missing on a call list for the owner or bookkeeper.
In early January, hand the finished sheet to your bookkeeper or accountant, or use it to file through the IRS's free IRIS portal.

blocks.h: Dates and numbers to know (checked at IRS.gov)
ul: For payments made in 2026, you report non-employee pay on Form 1099-NEC when it totals $2,000 or more for the year. For payments made before 2026 the threshold was $600, and the IRS says it will be adjusted for inflation after 2026.

Form 1099-NEC is due to both the IRS and the payee by January 31. When that falls on a weekend the deadline moves to the next business day, and January 31, 2027 is a Sunday, so the 2026 forms are due Monday, February 1, 2027.
If a payee doesn't give you a correct taxpayer ID, the IRS says you may have to hold back 24% of future payments (backup withholding).
If you file 10 or more information returns in total, you have to e-file. The IRS IRIS Taxpayer Portal is free and lets you upload a .csv file.
A W-9 contains a Social Security or taxpayer ID number. Keep it out of email threads, chat tools and AI tools. Store it in one access-controlled place.
Collect W-9s before you pay new contractors next year, so this becomes a one-time step per vendor.
Who counts as a contractor and which payments are reportable can be tricky. This recipe only gathers the paperwork; your accountant decides what gets filed.

pages.seoTitle: Freeze alert texts for HVAC and plumbing customers (NWS API)
pages.summary: Check the free National Weather Service API each afternoon for your service area. When a Freeze Warning, Hard Freeze Warning or Extreme Cold Warning is active, or the forecast low drops below a temperature you pick, send opted-in customers a short message with Red Cross frozen-pipe tips and your emergency number.
steps: List the ZIP codes or towns you serve and turn each into a latitude/longitude point (one per area is enough).

Every afternoon, have Zapier, Make or n8n call the National Weather Service API for active alerts at each point (api.weather.gov/alerts/active?point=LAT,LON). NWS asks every request to include a User-Agent header with your app name and a contact email.

Trigger when the alert is a Freeze Warning, Hard Freeze Warning, Wind Chill or Extreme Cold Warning. NWS issues Freeze Warnings mainly during the growing season, so also add a second trigger from the NWS forecast: a forecast low at or below a number you choose (for example 20°F).
Pull the matching customers from your CRM or field-service tool by service-area ZIP, and only those who agreed to get texts or emails from you.

Send one short message: what's coming, three pipe-protection steps from the Red Cross list below, and the number to call if a pipe freezes or the heat goes out. An AI step can shorten the wording, but the safety tips come from the Red Cross list, not the AI.
Log who was messaged and when, and don't send to the same customer again for 72 hours, so a multi-day cold snap doesn't flood them.
Give your dispatcher a heads-up in the same run so the on-call schedule is ready for no-heat and frozen-pipe calls.

p: Tools: the National Weather Service API (free, no key; it asks for a User-Agent header with contact info and has rate limits it doesn't publish, so poll a few points once or twice a day, not every minute), your CRM or field-service software, a texting or email tool, and Zapier/Make/n8n. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page.

blocks.h: What to put in the message (American Red Cross)
ul: Let cold water drip from faucets served by exposed pipes.
Open kitchen and bathroom cabinet doors so warmer air reaches the plumbing.
Keep garage doors closed if there are water lines in the garage.
Keep the thermostat at the same temperature day and night, and if you're leaving, no lower than 55°F.
Text only customers who agreed to get texts from you, and include a way to opt out.
Use the official alert wording and link to weather.gov. Don't predict the weather yourself or promise that pipes won't freeze.
Don't send space-heater or thawing advice beyond what the Red Cross page says. For a frozen pipe, tell people to call you or a plumber.
Test the alert filter against a few past cold days before turning on real sends.

pages.summary: Many health FSA plans end on December 31 and unused money can be lost. Each November, email patients who asked to hear from you a plain reminder to check their own FSA balance and deadline, with an easy link to book. The message never mentions their health details.

Have Zapier, Make or n8n send it through your practice's email tool, with one follow-up in early December only to people who haven't booked.

Money left after the plan year (or grace period) is lost, according to HealthCare.gov.
For 2026, the IRS limit on employee salary reductions to a health FSA is $3,400, up $100, and plans that allow a carryover can let up to $680 roll over.
Plan years and rules vary by employer, so the message should tell patients to check their own plan instead of naming a deadline.

pages.summary: Take Thanksgiving and holiday pre-orders through one form, then have the orders roll up each morning into a prep list by item and pickup day. The day before pickup, each guest gets a reminder with their pickup window and USDA food-safety basics for storing and reheating.
steps: Build one pre-order form (Google Forms, Jotform, or your POS's online ordering) with item, quantity, pickup date and time window, name, phone/email, and a checkbox for reminder texts or emails.
Send every order to one Google Sheet or Airtable base. Set an order cutoff date and a cap per pickup window so the kitchen isn't overbooked.
Every morning, have Zapier, Make or n8n total the orders by item and pickup day and send the kitchen a one-page prep list (print or email). Include the pickup-window counts for the front of house.
The day before pickup, send each guest who opted in one reminder: what they ordered, pickup time and place, and how to reach you if plans change.
Add a short food-safety note written from the USDA page below: refrigerate within 2 hours, reheat leftovers to 165°F, and use refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days.
On pickup day, mark orders as picked up from a simple checklist view, and send yourself a list of no-shows at closing so you can follow up the next morning.
After the holiday, compare what you prepped with what was picked up so next year's caps and par levels start from your own numbers.

blocks.h: Food-safety basics to put in the reminder (USDA FSIS)
ul: Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours of cooking or of taking food out of a warming appliance (1 hour if it's above 90°F).
Bacteria grow fastest between 40°F and 140°F. Keep hot food at 140°F or warmer and cold food at 40°F or below.
Reheat leftovers to 165°F, checked with a food thermometer. Bring sauces, soups and gravies to a rolling boil.
Refrigerated leftovers keep 3 to 4 days. Frozen leftovers keep 3 to 4 months for best quality.
Text only guests who checked the box to get texts, and include a way to opt out.
Use your own kitchen's reheating instructions for each dish. The USDA notes are general, so don't let an AI step invent cooking times.
Put allergen information next to each item on the form (see the allergen recipe) and don't promise a dish is allergen-free unless your kitchen can guarantee it.

blocks.h: Gift card rules to know (CFPB and Federal Reserve, Regulation E)

Under federal law, inactivity fees can only be charged after 12 months with no activity, and only if the fee is clearly disclosed on the card. No more than one such fee can be charged per month.
Fees and expiration terms must be disclosed before purchase. If a card itself expires before the funds do, the card must say how to get a free replacement.
Simplest path: no fees and no expiration date. Ask your POS provider how its gift cards handle this, and check your state's rules.
Don't email a recipient's gift card code to anyone except the address the buyer entered.

pages.seoTitle: Critical PHP update, Oct 2026: what small business sites should do
pages.summary: On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 to fix two critical flaws that can let an attacker run code on a web server without logging in. If your website runs on PHP (most WordPress and many hosted sites do), ask your host or developer to confirm it's updated. It's a five-minute email.

p: Peace of mind that your website, contact forms and customer data aren't sitting on a server with a known critical hole, going into your busiest season, without touching any server settings yourself.

ul: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The PHP team strongly encourages all users to update immediately.
The PHP team says all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, and calls the risk highest for Apache with mod_php.
For each release the team says: "There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice."
Linux distributions and long-term support vendors got the patches in advance, so many hosts can update quickly.
PHP 8.1 and older no longer get updates from the PHP project. PHP 8.2 gets security fixes only until December 31, 2026.
On October 23 the PHP team added an informational advisory suggesting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next bugfix release, to close an unlikely extra attack path.

ol: Find out if your site uses PHP. If it's WordPress, it does. In WordPress, go to Tools > Site Health > Info > Server to see the PHP version; the Status tab flags an outdated PHP version as a security issue.

Email your web host or developer: "Please confirm our site is running PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 or later (or a vendor-patched build for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), and tell me which version we're on."
If you're on PHP 8.1 or older, ask for a plan to move to a supported version. WordPress recommends PHP 8.3 or greater.
If you're on PHP 8.2, ask about moving up before it reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.
While you're at it, make sure your hosting and website admin logins use multifactor authentication, and that WordPress plugins and themes are set to update.

ul: Don't change server or php.ini settings yourself. Ask your host or developer, and test the site after any update.
Some hosts patch PHP in the background with their own builds, so the version number may look different. Ask them to confirm in writing that these two CVEs are fixed.
Ignore scary emails that offer to "fix" your site for a fee. Talk only to your own host or developer.

Sites built entirely on platforms like Shopify, Squarespace or Wix are managed by the platform, so there's usually nothing to do. Still, any separate WordPress blog or landing pages you host yourself should be checked.

steps: Make a simple vendor contact sheet (Google Sheets or Airtable) with each vendor's known phone number, taken from a contract or past invoice, not from a new email.

Keyword rules miss some scams. Train staff that any request to change where money goes gets a call, flagged or not.

blocks.h: Protect your gift cards from card draining
p: Card draining is a gift card scam aimed at generic gift cards hanging on open racks at grocery stores, pharmacies and big-box stores. A thief takes a card off the rack, scratches or peels the cover to copy the card number and PIN (or puts a fake barcode sticker over the real one), reseals it and puts it back. When a shopper buys the card and loads money on it, the thief spends the balance online, often before the gift is ever opened.
ul: If you sell your own gift cards: this is a strong reason to sell direct. Offer e-gift cards from your own website, and keep physical cards behind the counter so they're only activated at your register when someone pays.
Keep any physical cards you sell out of open, self-serve racks. If a reseller stocks your cards, ask how they store and protect them.
Tell your customers the safest way to buy is straight from you, in person or on your website. It protects them and keeps the sale with your business.

Buyer tips: buy direct from the business or online from the brand's own site. In a store, check the back of the card for torn, wrinkled or resealed packaging, a scratched or exposed PIN, or a barcode sticker, and pick a different card if anything looks off.
Keep the receipt and a photo of the card. Register the card if the issuer allows it, check the balance right away, and give the gift soon so it's used before anyone else can drain it.
If a card has no money on it, contact the card issuer and the store where you bought it right away. Paying by credit card can give you more ways to get your money back.

pages.summary: If your domain name lapses or your site's security certificate expires, customers see an error page or nothing at all, often in your busiest week. Certificates now expire faster: since March 15, 2026 the industry maximum is 200 days, dropping to 100 days in March 2027. This recipe keeps one list of your renewal dates and sends you alerts 30, 14 and 3 days before anything runs out.
steps: List every domain you own and every website on it in a Google Sheet: domain, registrar, renewal date, whether auto-renew is on, the card on file, and who has the login.

Log in to your registrar, turn on auto-renew for every domain you want to keep, and make sure the card and contact email are current. ICANN requires registrars to send renewal reminders about a month and a week before expiry, so those emails must reach an inbox someone reads.
Ask your web host or website builder whether your certificate renews automatically. Most hosts and builders do this for you; if yours doesn't, ask them to set it up.
Set up a free or low-cost certificate monitoring service (Let's Encrypt lists options) or a daily Zapier, Make or n8n check that reads each site's certificate expiry date into the sheet.
Send an alert to the owner and your web person at 30, 14 and 3 days before any domain or certificate expires, and an urgent alert if a certificate's days left suddenly drop without a renewal.
Once a quarter, open your site in a private browser window on your phone to confirm the padlock shows and there's no warning page.

p: Tools: your domain registrar account, your web host or website builder, a Google Sheet, and optionally a certificate monitoring service or Zapier/Make/n8n. Costs: see each vendor's current pricing page.

ul: The CA/Browser Forum's Ballot SC-081v3 cut the maximum lifetime of public website certificates to 200 days for certificates issued on or after March 15, 2026, then 100 days from March 15, 2027 and 47 days from March 15, 2029.
Let's Encrypt stopped sending certificate expiration reminder emails on June 4, 2025, and recommends a third-party monitoring service if you want them.
Let's Encrypt plans to move its default certificates from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027 and 45 days on February 16, 2028, and says manual renewal is not recommended.

ICANN's Expired Registration Recovery Policy requires registrars of generic domains (like .com) to send at least two reminders before expiry, about one month and one week ahead, and another within five days after it expires.
Don't rely on renewal emails alone. An old address, a full inbox or a spam filter means nobody sees them.
Keep registrar logins in a password manager the business controls, not in a former employee's or web designer's personal account.
An expired card is the most common reason auto-renew fails. Put the card's expiry date in the sheet too.
Country-code domains (like .us or .co) may follow different renewal rules; check your registrar's terms.

pages.summary: Holiday giveaways and "leave us a review, get 10% off" offers are tempting, but Google's rules don't allow offering any discount, freebie or payment in exchange for a review, or asking only your happy customers. p: Reviews that stay up, and a Business Profile that keeps collecting new ones through the holidays, instead of reviews that get removed or a warning on your listing during your busiest season.

ul: Google's Maps contribution policy says merchants may not offer incentives, such as payment, discounts, free goods or services, in exchange for posting a review, or for changing or removing a negative one.

The same policy says merchants may not discourage negative reviews or selectively ask only happy customers for positive ones, and shouldn't pressure customers to review while they're on the premises or ask for specific wording.
Google says reviews posted because of an incentive are not allowed and will be removed.

If Google finds a business broke its Fake Engagement policy, it may, beyond removing reviews, block new reviews for a set time, unpublish existing reviews for a set time, or show customers a warning that fake reviews were removed. Google says it emails the owner first, and owners can appeal.

ol: Read through your holiday plans: social giveaways, Small Business Saturday offers, receipts, table cards, email footers and staff scripts. Remove anything that links a review to a prize, entry, discount or freebie.

Tools that send only 4- and 5-star customers to Google and route everyone else to a private form are selective soliciting. Send everyone to the same place.

steps: Find the domain your email tool signs mail with (the DKIM d= domain or the SPF Return-Path domain). Your email provider’s domain-setup page shows it.
Sign in to Google Postmaster Tools on a computer, add that domain, and verify it by pasting the TXT or CNAME record Google gives you into your DNS. Dashboards stay empty until the domain is verified.
Give a second trusted person read access in Postmaster Tools (Manage users) so alerts are not tied to one inbox.

Each Monday, open the spam-rate dashboard—or have an automation do it. Developers or a builder can connect the Postmaster Tools API to Zapier, Make, n8n or a small script that pulls the latest daily spam rate.
Set two alert levels: a heads-up if the rate goes above 0.10%, and an urgent alert at 0.20% so you act well before Google’s 0.30% ceiling. Send the alert to email or Slack with the date range.
When an alert fires, write down what changed in the days before: a new signup form or list source, a bigger or more frequent send, a new offer type. Undo or slow the most recent change first.
Make unsubscribing easy (one-click unsubscribe and a visible link), confirm new signups, and stop mailing people who never open—then watch the next several reported days before sending more.
Keep a one-line log of each alert and the fix you made, so next holiday season you know which list sources caused trouble.

ul: Google’s Email sender guidelines tell senders to keep the spam rate reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.10% and to avoid ever reaching 0.30% or higher.

Google says dashboard data is not real time (typically updated within 24 hours), uses UTC, and may be missing on low-volume days to protect user privacy.
Google’s Postmaster Tools API lets you pull these statistics, including spam rate and compliance status, into other systems.

p: Audience Bridge, a newsletter-monitoring company, wrote on November 4, 2026 that after it pushed more co-registration signups into one of its own newsletters, Gmail’s reported spam rate stayed above 0.30% for four days. It cut that signup volume in half first and kept watching. This is one publisher’s account, written by a vendor; use it as a pattern (check what changed before complaints rose), not as a benchmark.

ul: Small lists may never show data, because Google hides low-volume days. If you send only a few hundred emails a week to Gmail users, rely on unsubscribe and reply trends instead.
Your email tool’s complaint number is not Gmail’s number. Yahoo and others send complaint feedback to providers; Gmail reports an aggregate rate in Postmaster Tools.
Treat 0.30% as a hard limit, not a target. Aim to stay under 0.10% so a single bad send doesn’t push you over.

blocks.h: How to do it (about an hour before each campaign)
ul: List only the pages your ads point to: the landing page, the product or category pages, cart and checkout.

Collect evidence: a phone screenshot and a desktop screenshot of each page, the page text, and a free crawl or audit report (Google Lighthouse is built into Chrome; crawler tools such as Screaming Frog have a limited free version).

Give your AI assistant one specific job, in your own words. For example: “Check these pages for broken links, offers that don’t match, items shown as available that are sold out, missing product details and mobile layout problems. For each, give the URL, the evidence and how it would affect a shopper. Mark anything you could not confirm. Do not claim you clicked or checked out. Do not change the site.”
Add your real campaign details—sale dates, discount code or automatic discount, shipping cutoff—so the AI can spot contradictions.

Then do the human part: on your phone and on a computer, open the menu, pick a size or color, add to cart and place a test order. Confirm the sale shows up correctly in your ad platform’s conversion report.
Sort the findings by customer impact. A checkout failure beats a spacing glitch. Fix the top items, then re-check before the ads go live.

pages.summary: Holiday shoppers check return rules before they buy, and Black Friday ads that promise “easy returns” have to match what your store actually does. Shopify’s Terms of Service require a current, public refund policy that is easy to find. Write down your real rules, set them in Settings → Policies, publish the written return and refund policy (automated or edited by you), link it in your menu, and read your ads against it before Cyber Week (Thanksgiving November 26 through Cyber Monday November 30).
steps: Write down the rules you will actually follow this season: how many days customers have, whether the window starts on purchase, shipment or delivery, who pays return shipping, any restocking fee, what counts as final sale, how gift returns work, and whether you will extend the window for holiday purchases.

In Shopify, go to Settings → Policies. Under Return and cancellation rules, turn on return rules and set the return window, return shipping (free, a flat fee, or the customer buys a label), an optional restocking-fee percentage, and any final-sale products or collections.

Optional: add a return-window override for specific collections (for example a shorter window on sale items) and cancellation rules for unfulfilled orders if you want customers to be able to cancel before something ships.

Open the written Return and refund policy in the Written policies section. You can turn on Use automated policy so the text stays in sync with those return rules, or turn automation off and write or edit the policy yourself. Shopify’s help pages say you are responsible for reviewing it before you save.

Check the published policy against Shopify’s refund-policy checklist: the time a product must be returned, the address it should be sent to, who pays to return it, that refund timing can depend on where the customer lives, and contact details if a refund is delayed. Shopify’s 2026 return-policy guide also recommends stating item condition, refund vs. exchange vs. store credit, how to start a return, processing time, and exceptions (gifts, damaged items, international orders, final sale), including any holiday extension.

Policies are automatically linked in the checkout footer, and a return-policy link appears on the order review page. Also add the policy to a store menu (Content → Menus) so shoppers can find it before checkout. The page lives at /policies/refund-policy on your domain.
If you want customers to start returns themselves, go to Settings → Customer accounts and turn on Self-serve returns and cancellations, then add the customer-accounts URL to your policy or footer.

Read every Black Friday, Small Business Saturday and Cyber Monday ad, email and landing-page line against the published policy. If an ad says “free returns” or “hassle-free exchanges,” the policy must say the same thing.
Brief whoever will handle December returns, and process one test return in admin (Orders → an order → Return) so shipping-label and refund steps match what customers will read.

p: A Shopify admin login with access to Settings → Policies (and Customer accounts if you use self-serve returns). Owners on other platforms should publish the same information on their site using that platform’s policy tools—the checklist still applies. This is not legal advice; Shopify says to consult a lawyer if you need help deciding what the law requires.

ul: Shopify’s consumer-protection help page says that under Shopify’s Terms of Service you must provide current, accurate, public-facing and easy-to-access information about your refund policy, including the return time window, the return address, who pays to return an item, that refund timing may depend on the customer’s location, and contact information if a refund is delayed.

Return and cancellation rules are set in Settings → Policies. Return rules cover fulfilled items (window, shipping cost, restocking fee, final-sale exceptions and optional window overrides). Cancellation rules cover unfulfilled items. Changes apply to future orders, not orders already placed.

You can publish an automated return and refund policy that uses those settings and updates when they change, or write the policy yourself. After you add store policies they are automatically linked in the checkout footer. Shopify also recommends linking them in your store menus. A direct link uses /policies/refund-policy on your domain.

Shopify’s 2026 “How To Write a Return Policy” guide includes a writing checklist and notes that you can mention holiday or promotion extensions in the return-window section. It tells you to publish the policy where customers can find it before they buy.
Self-serve returns and cancellations are turned on separately under Settings → Customer accounts. Customers can submit requests only for items that are eligible under your rules.

This page is a how-to for publishing what you already decided—not legal advice. Consumer-protection rules vary by where you and your customers are, and Shopify says you remain responsible for following applicable laws.
Do not promise in ads what the policy does not allow. Shopify also warns against marketing claims that are not true (for example a fake limited-stock notice).

Automated policy text may not cover subscriptions, regulated products or every market you sell to. Review it whenever your practices change. If you sell to customers in the European Union, Shopify documents extra withdrawal settings; review those pages with a legal advisor rather than copying another store’s policy.

If you run the business from home, the published policy may show a contact address. Shopify notes that some disclosures require a physical business address and that you should use business contact details you are comfortable making public.
Return fees are not automatically deducted from refunds; Shopify says you need to deduct applicable fees when you create the refund.

pages.seoTitle: Tell AI tools who you serve and how you price (2026 tip)
pages.summary: Some holiday shoppers now ask ChatGPT, Copilot or Google’s AI answers to suggest a shop, salon or contractor. Those tools summarize your website and listings in their own words. A study published by Search Engine Land on November 5, 2026 scored about 2,000 brand mentions across four AI engines in one software category and found they usually got what a business does right, were shakier on who it is for, and often invented missing details—most often prices. Close those gaps yourself: one plain sentence on who you serve, where, and how pricing works, repeated everywhere you are listed.

p: AI answers and first-time visitors that describe your business the way you would—who it is for, the area you cover and how pricing works—instead of a guess. That makes it more likely the right holiday shoppers pick you and fewer wrong-fit inquiries show up.

blocks.h: How to do it (about an hour)
ul: Write your ground truth in four short lines: what you do, who it is for (for example “families in Midtown looking for handmade gifts under $50” or “homeowners within 20 miles of Springfield”), what makes you different, and one proof point you can back up (years in business, a real award, a real review count).

Add a pricing line. If you publish prices, show them. If you price by quote, say so and give the rule: “Pricing is by quote and depends on room size and materials; most kitchen refreshes start at a site visit.” The study found engines repeated that kind of conditional sentence when brands published it.

Put the who-it’s-for sentence near the top of your homepage and About page in plain text (not inside an image), and use the same wording in your Google Business Profile description, Yelp page, Facebook page and any directory you control.
Keep one differentiator and repeat it the same way everywhere. The study found a single clear, consistently repeated message held up best; vague or mixed messages got blurred.

Check what AI tools say: ask two or three assistants “What is [your business] in [your town], who is it for, and what does it cost?” Ask more than once, because answers change between runs. Note anything wrong—especially prices, hours or services you do not offer.
Fix your own pages and listings first so the correct facts are easy to find. If a wrong fact traces to a third-party directory, update or claim that listing too.
Recheck after any price or service change, and before Black Friday (November 27) and Small Business Saturday (November 28).

p: The study looked at one business-software category (dental practice software), not local shops, so treat it as a direction, not a promise about your results. We are not repeating its percentages. Only publish prices, proof points and service areas that are true and that you will honor; do not invent awards or review counts. No AI tool is guaranteed to recommend you or describe you correctly, and anyone who promises a “rank in ChatGPT” is overselling. You do not need to paste customer data into an AI tool to do any of this.

pages.seoTitle: Back-in-stock alerts for holiday best-sellers (Klaviyo how-to)
pages.summary: When a holiday best-seller sells out, shoppers who wanted it usually leave. A back-in-stock form puts a “Notify me” button on sold-out product pages and lets them ask for an email or text when it returns. In Klaviyo (with Shopify or BigCommerce), you build a back-in-stock flow that waits until the item is restocked, then publish a back-in-stock form. Set it up before Black Friday (November 27) so sold-out items keep collecting interested buyers.
steps: Check you can use it: Klaviyo’s built-in back-in-stock form works for stores with an enabled Shopify or BigCommerce integration, and Klaviyo onsite tracking must be installed on your storefront. Other platforms use Klaviyo’s back-in-stock flow installation guide instead.

Build the flow first. In Klaviyo go to Flows → Create flow, search the library for “back in stock,” and pick a template (or build your own triggered by the Klaviyo metric Subscribed to Back in Stock, with no trigger or profile filters).
Keep the Back in stock delay directly after the trigger. Subscribers wait there until their item is restocked; you do not need extra time delays.

Use one notification message. Klaviyo recommends turning Smart Sending off for it so a recent email does not cause the alert to be skipped. Preview it to make sure it shows the right product, then set the message to Live—messages left in Draft do not send.

Create the form: Sign-up forms → Create form → search “back in stock” and choose a template. Choose whether the “Notify me” button replaces the Add to cart button or sits beneath it, and match the styling to your store.

Decide on channels. Email is the simplest. If you add a phone field for text or WhatsApp alerts, finish that channel’s setup first and keep the required consent and disclosure language—Klaviyo says explicit consent is required and cannot be made optional.
On Shopify, optionally use Targeting with product tags so the button only appears on products you will actually restock this season. Then publish the form.

After the first sign-up is recorded, open Back in stock settings (account Settings → Other, or from the delay step) and set a minimum restock quantity and how many people to notify per batch, so 300 people are not alerted when 3 units arrive.
Test with a real product: mark a variant out of stock, sign up with your own email, restock it and confirm the alert arrives.

p: Tools: Shopify or BigCommerce store + Klaviyo with onsite tracking installed. Shopify’s app store also has other back-in-stock apps; the steps differ but the idea is the same. Costs: see each vendor’s current pricing page.

ul: Klaviyo’s back-in-stock form shows a customizable “Notify me” button on product pages when the selected variant is out of stock and matches your targeting; the button appears and disappears with your inventory.

Shoppers can sign up by email, text message or WhatsApp depending on your setup. An optional checkbox can also ask for promotional email consent; for texts and WhatsApp, explicit consent and disclosure language are required.

Submitting the form logs a Subscribed to Back in Stock event. A flow triggered by that metric, with a Back in stock delay, sends the alert once the item meets your inventory and notification settings.
You can only have one back-in-stock form in your account at a time. If you installed Klaviyo’s older back-in-stock code snippet, remove it first to avoid duplicate buttons.

Back in stock settings cover minimum inventory rules and how many customers to notify and how long to wait between batches; the settings tab appears only after at least one Subscribed to Back in Stock event.
If you use Shopify POS and sell online, Klaviyo counts in-store and warehouse inventory together, so a unit sitting on your shop shelf can trigger an online alert.
Klaviyo cannot recheck inventory before a second message, so keep the flow to one alert rather than a reminder series.

Only offer alerts on items you really expect to restock before the gift deadline, and say so on the page (“Back in early December”) if you know. Do not use the alert list for unrelated promotions unless the shopper also opted in to marketing.
Text alerts follow the same consent and quiet-hours rules as your other texts; see our holiday texting tip.
